Archduke Franz Ferdinand. The heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, shot and killed on June 28, 1914, in Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb member of the revolutionary group Black Hand.

Franz Ferdinand was riding in an open-topped motorcar with his wife, Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg, when Princip fired. Both the archduke and his wife were killed. The chauffeur was also struck. Princip was only nineteen years old and a Bosnian Serb nationalist opposed to Austro-Hungarian rule.

This assassination was part of a coordinated plot. Multiple would-be assassins had been positioned along the motorcade route. In fact, Franz Ferdinand's motorcade had actually escaped an earlier bomb attempt that same morning before Princip's gun succeeded. Princip belonged to Black Hand, a Serbian nationalist secret society dedicated to liberating Slavic lands from Austro-Hungarian control. He was captured immediately and died in prison in 1918.

Austria-Hungary issued a harsh ultimatum to Serbia, blaming it for the assassination. When Serbia defied the ultimatum, Austria-Hungary mobilized. Russia mobilized to defend Serbia. Germany sided with Austria-Hungary, and France sided with Russia. The alliance system and rigid mobilization schedules transformed this regional Balkan crisis into a general European war by August 1914.

The date June 28, 1914, marks the boundary between the long nineteenth century and the catastrophic twentieth. No other assassination has triggered such immediate and inexorable geopolitical consequences. Within six weeks of Princip's shots, millions were mobilizing for war. The event also highlights the role of contingency: the archduke's motorcade took a wrong turn that morning, putting Princip directly in its path after several earlier assassination attempts had failed. In Western literature and drama, from Shakespeare to modern times, the betrayal of trusted leaders has resonated through generations, and this moment stands as the canonical example of how a single violent act by one person can reshape the world.
